title: Threat Modeling a Modern Web Application
content:
Threat modeling asks what could go wrong with a specific system and which changes would reduce that risk. A modern web application has several trust boundaries: browser to API, API to database, service to service, and administrator to privileged operation. A diagram that shows these flows can reveal a missing authorization check faster than a generic list of attacks. The output should be a set of decisions, owners, and verification tasks, not a decorative security document.

Choose a bounded system and decision

Start with a feature, not the entire company. Define what is in scope: a password reset flow, file upload service, or checkout API. Name the assets that matter, such as account access, customer records, payment intent, or service availability. Record the intended users and what each may do. Include assumptions about identity providers, hosting, and third-party services; an assumption that changes later can invalidate a threat decision.

The OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet describes a repeatable process of modeling the application, identifying threats, choosing mitigations, and reviewing the result. Its guidance also notes that threat modeling should be revisited as systems change. Use this as a working rhythm: a small model reviewed at design time, then updated when a boundary or privilege changes.

Draw data flow and trust boundaries

Sketch actors, processes, data stores, and external services. Draw arrows with the data carried and the authority used. Mark where data crosses from a less trusted context to a more trusted one. A browser can submit a user identifier, but the server must decide whether the authenticated user may act on that identifier. A queue message may come from another service, yet its payload may still contain untrusted customer input.

Do not omit operational paths: background jobs, webhooks, support tools, exports, backups, and administrative endpoints. Those paths often have broader permissions than the ordinary UI. Mark where secrets are obtained and where logs receive data. The diagram need not use a formal notation if the team can read it, but every arrow should have a concrete purpose and owner.

Ask specific abuse questions

At each boundary, ask who can impersonate a caller, alter data, read something private, repeat a request, exhaust capacity, or act with more privilege than intended. For a file upload, consider content type confusion, oversized files, malware handling, storage access, and whether a returned URL exposes private material. For a password reset, consider token guessing, expiry, reuse, account enumeration, and whether old sessions remain active after recovery. These are prompts for analysis, not a claim that every feature has every threat.

Trace at least one abuse path end to end. If a webhook accepts a signed event, where is the signature checked? What happens if the same event is delivered twice? Can a valid event reference another customer’s object? Threats often cross multiple components, so a control at only one layer may be insufficient. Include failures and exceptions: a timeout during an authorization lookup must not turn into default allow.

Turn threats into verifiable controls

Write a control next to each high-priority threat and state how it will be checked. The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard offers structured security requirements that teams can use to specify and test application controls. Choose relevant requirements; do not treat a checklist as proof that the particular data flow is safe. For an object access risk, the control might be server-side ownership validation on every read and write, with tests for cross-user identifiers.

Risk ranking should consider plausible impact and exposure in the actual system. A public unauthenticated endpoint that can alter billing records warrants different urgency from a low-value internal report with no external entry point. Record the rationale and uncertainty rather than assigning an unexplained number. Sometimes the response is to remove a feature or reduce stored data rather than add another filter.

A hypothetical appointment API

Imagine a hypothetical appointment service. Patients create bookings, clinicians view assigned schedules, and an integration sends reminder events. The team draws the browser-to-API path, the booking database, and a queue worker that contacts the reminder provider. A developer notices that the reminder worker accepts a booking identifier from a queue message but does not verify which tenant owns it. The threat is cross-tenant disclosure if a compromised integration or malformed message references another tenant’s booking.

The team narrows the queue publisher’s permissions, makes the worker load the booking within the expected tenant context, adds a negative integration test, and limits reminder payload fields. They record an assumption that the reminder provider retains messages for a stated period and assign someone to verify it. This is a hypothetical example and reports no real exploit or test result. Its value is showing how an ordinary feature diagram can expose a privileged background path.

Maintain the model alongside the feature

Store the diagram and decision notes near the design or code. When a new provider, permission, endpoint, or data category is added, review the affected arrows and assumptions. A model that never changes becomes misleading. Close each action with evidence: test result, configuration review, or documented risk acceptance by the appropriate owner. If a mitigation is deferred, state the reason and review date.

Threat-model checklist

  • Scope one feature and name its assets and actors.
  • Draw data flows, stores, external services, and trust boundaries.
  • Include background and administrative paths.
  • Trace plausible abuse and failure paths end to end.
  • Rank risks with context and uncertainty.
  • Map each priority risk to a control and verification.
  • Assign owners and revisit after material changes.
excerpt: Threat model a web feature by mapping data flows and trust boundaries, tracing realistic abuse paths, and assigning testable controls with owners.
